title: Bonding, Color and Magnetism of Complexes
description: Crystal field and ligand field theory, spin states, Jahn–Teller distortion, magnetism and electronic spectra.
overview: Why is [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ violet and [Zn(H₂O)₆]²⁺ colorless? Why is [Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺ paramagnetic with four unpaired electrons, while [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ is diamagnetic? Why are Ni(II) and Pt(II) complexes of the same formula tetrahedral or square planar? The answers lie in how the five d orbitals of the metal respond to the surrounding ligands.

This chapter develops crystal field theory, then the more complete ligand field theory based on molecular orbitals. It applies them to the splitting of d orbitals in octahedral, tetrahedral and square planar complexes, high-spin and low-spin configurations, Jahn–Teller distortions, magnetic properties and the UV–visible spectra that give complexes their colors.
objectives: Draw the d-orbital splitting for octahedral, tetrahedral and square planar fields.
Calculate the ligand field stabilization energy and predict high-spin or low-spin configurations.
Use the spectrochemical series, and explain it with π-donor and π-acceptor effects.
Calculate spin-only magnetic moments and describe types of magnetic behavior, including spin crossover.
Interpret d–d and charge-transfer spectra, and relate absorbed wavelength to observed color and Δ.

sections.title: Crystal field theory for octahedral complexes
body: In **crystal field theory (CFT)** the ligands are treated as point negative charges, and the question is how they repel the metal’s d electrons. In a free ion the five d orbitals have the same energy. In an octahedral field, with ligands on the ±x, ±y, ±z axes, the two orbitals that point at the ligands, d_{z²} and d_{x²−y²} (the **e_g** set), are repelled more and rise in energy, and the three that point between the ligands, d_{xy}, d_{xz} and d_{yz} (the **t₂g** set), are repelled less and fall. The gap is the **crystal field splitting Δₒ**. The average energy (barycenter) is unchanged, so e_g is raised by 0.6Δₒ and t₂g lowered by 0.4Δₒ.

body.caption: Octahedral crystal field splitting. The t₂g set (three orbitals) lies 0.4Δₒ below the barycenter, and the e_g set (two orbitals) lies 0.6Δₒ above it.

body: Electrons fill the lower t₂g set first, which lowers the energy of the complex. The **ligand field stabilization energy (LFSE)** is the net lowering: LFSE = (−0.4 n_{t₂g} + 0.6 n_{e_g}) Δₒ, plus the energy cost P for each extra electron pair beyond those in the free ion.

For d⁴ to d⁷ configurations there are two ways to fill the orbitals. A **weak field** (Δₒ < P, the **pairing energy**) leaves electrons unpaired in both sets: **high-spin**. A **strong field** (Δₒ > P) fills the t₂g set completely first: **low-spin**. The d¹–d³ and d⁸–d¹⁰ configurations have only one possible arrangement.

body: Δₒ depends on both the ligand and the metal. The ligands in order of increasing field strength (the **spectrochemical series**) are:

body.eq: I⁻ < Br⁻ < S²⁻ < SCN⁻ < Cl⁻ < NO₃⁻ < F⁻ < OH⁻ < C₂O₄²⁻ < H₂O < NCS⁻ < NH₃ < en < bipy < phen < NO₂⁻ < PPh₃ < CN⁻ < CO

body: For metals, Δₒ increases with oxidation state (Fe²⁺ 10,400 cm⁻¹, Fe³⁺ 13,700 cm⁻¹ with water) and down a group (the 4d and 5d metals have a Δ 30–50% larger than 3d), so nearly all 4d and 5d octahedral complexes are low-spin. Weak-field ligands (halides, H₂O) give high-spin 3d complexes, and strong-field ligands (CN⁻, CO, phen) give low-spin ones.

example.title: Spin state and LFSE
example.problem: Give the electron configuration, number of unpaired electrons and LFSE of [Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺ (Δₒ = 10,400 cm⁻¹, P about 17,600 cm⁻¹) and [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ (Δₒ about 33,000 cm⁻¹).
solution: Both contain Fe²⁺ (d⁶). With water, Δₒ < P, so high spin: t₂g⁴e_g² with 4 unpaired electrons, LFSE = −0.4Δₒ = −4,200 cm⁻¹.
With cyanide, Δₒ > P, so low spin: t₂g⁶, no unpaired electrons (diamagnetic), LFSE = −2.4Δₒ + 2P = −79,200 + 35,200 = −44,000 cm⁻¹.

sections.title: Tetrahedral and square planar fields, and Jahn–Teller distortion
body: In a **tetrahedral** field the splitting is inverted and smaller: the e set (d_{z²}, d_{x²−y²}) lies below the t₂ set (d_{xy}, d_{xz}, d_{yz}), since the ligands point between the axes and approach the t₂ orbitals more closely. With fewer ligands (4 against 6) and a poorer overlap, **Δₜ = (4/9)Δₒ**, which is always smaller than the pairing energy, so tetrahedral complexes are always high spin. They are favored for d⁰, d⁵ (high spin) and d¹⁰ ions, which have no LFSE preference for octahedral geometry, and by bulky ligands: [ZnCl₄]²⁻, [FeCl₄]⁻, [CoCl₄]²⁻ (blue), [NiCl₄]²⁻.

In a **square planar** field the ligands lie on the x and y axes only, and d_{x²−y²} is raised far above the others. The ordering is d_{x²−y²} ≫ d_{xy} > d_{z²} > d_{xz}, d_{yz}. For d⁸ ions with strong-field ligands, the eight electrons fill the four lower orbitals and leave d_{x²−y²} empty, a large stabilization: [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻, [PtCl₄]²⁻, [PdCl₄]²⁻, Rh(I), Ir(I) (Vaska’s complex), Au(III). The 4d and 5d d⁸ ions are always square planar since their Δ is large, while Ni(II) is tetrahedral with weak ligands ([NiCl₄]²⁻, paramagnetic) and square planar with strong ligands ([Ni(CN)₄]²⁻, diamagnetic).

The **Jahn–Teller theorem** says that a nonlinear molecule in an electronically degenerate state distorts to remove the degeneracy and lower its energy. In octahedral complexes, uneven occupation of the e_g set produces a large distortion, and uneven occupation of t₂g produces only a small one:

head: Configuration
Degenerate orbitals unevenly filled?
Distortion
Examples
rows: [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺: four short and two long bonds
d¹, d², d⁴ low spin, d⁵ low spin, d⁶ high spin, d⁷ high spin
table.caption: Jahn–Teller distortions of octahedral complexes.

body: The commonest distortion is **tetragonal elongation**: the two axial bonds lengthen, so d_{z²} drops (and d_{x²−y²} rises), and the extra energy gained by filling d_{z²} twice and d_{x²−y²} once is the stabilization. Copper(II) complexes are almost always elongated, and the distortion contributes to the high stability of Cu(II) in the Irving–Williams series.

sections.title: Ligand field theory: σ and π bonding
body: Crystal field theory explains the splitting but treats bonding as purely electrostatic, so it cannot explain why neutral CO and the anion CN⁻ are strong-field ligands and the anion F⁻ is weak. **Ligand field theory (LFT)** applies molecular orbital theory to the metal–ligand bonds. The σ-donor orbitals of the six ligands form symmetry-adapted combinations of a₁g, e_g and t₁ᵤ symmetry that combine with the metal’s 4s, 3d (e_g) and 4p orbitals, giving six bonding MOs, mostly ligand-based and holding the twelve ligand electrons. The metal’s d_{xy}, d_{xz} and d_{yz} (t₂g) have no σ match and remain nonbonding. The antibonding e_g* orbitals, mostly metal d_{z²} and d_{x²−y²}, lie above. The **ligand field splitting Δₒ is the gap between t₂g and e_g***, which the metal’s d electrons fill.
Adding π interactions between the ligands and the t₂g orbitals explains the spectrochemical series:

list: **π-donor ligands** (F⁻, Cl⁻, OH⁻, H₂O, with filled p orbitals) interact with the metal t₂g set, pushing it **up**, and so *reduce* Δₒ. These are weak-field ligands.

**π-acceptor ligands** (CO, CN⁻, PR₃, bipy, with empty π* or d orbitals) accept electron density from filled metal t₂g orbitals (**back-bonding**), lowering them, and so *increase* Δₒ. These are the strong-field ligands.
Pure σ-donors (NH₃, en) lie in between.

body: The back-bonding in a metal carbonyl has a vivid signature in IR spectra: the extent of back-donation into the CO π* orbital weakens the C–O bond, so the CO stretch falls from 2143 cm⁻¹ (free CO) to about 2000 cm⁻¹ in [Cr(CO)₆] and 1850 cm⁻¹ in [V(CO)₆]⁻ (see the chapter on organometallic chemistry).

check.q: Why is CO a strong-field ligand?
check.a: It is a π-acceptor, and back-donation stabilizes the t₂g set

check.q: In ligand field theory, Δₒ is the gap between…
check.a: The nonbonding t₂g and the antibonding e_g* orbitals
wrong: The bonding a₁g and t₁ᵤ orbitals
The ligand and metal s orbitals

sections.title: Magnetic properties
body: A species with unpaired electrons is attracted into a magnetic field (**paramagnetism**), and one with all electrons paired is weakly repelled (**diamagnetism**). The size of the effect, the **magnetic susceptibility** χ, is measured with a **Gouy balance** (the apparent weight change of a sample in a field), with the Evans NMR method (the shift of a reference signal), or with a **SQUID** magnetometer. It is expressed as the effective magnetic moment, in units of the **Bohr magneton**, μ_B. For a first-row complex whose moment comes from spin alone, the **spin-only formula** gives

body.eq: μ_so = √(n(n + 2)) μ_B     (n = number of unpaired electrons)

body: The measured moment tells the number of unpaired electrons, and so distinguishes high- and low-spin complexes: [Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺ (d⁶ high spin, 4 unpaired, μ ≈ 5.3 μ_B) against [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ (0 unpaired, diamagnetic). Moments of t₂g configurations (d¹, d², d⁶ and d⁷ high spin) are higher than the spin-only value because of an **orbital contribution**, which is quenched in e_g-filled configurations (d³, d⁸ and high-spin d⁵ come close to spin-only).

In solids, the unpaired spins of neighboring atoms can interact. In **ferromagnetism** (Fe, Co, Ni, CrO₂) the spins align parallel and give a large permanent magnetization. In **antiferromagnetism** (MnO, Cr₂O₃, many Cu(II) dimers) neighbors align antiparallel and the net moment cancels below the Néel temperature. In **ferrimagnetism** (magnetite, Fe₃O₄, ferrites) antiparallel spins of unequal size leave a net moment.

When Δₒ is close to the pairing energy, as for some Fe(II) (d⁶) complexes with N-donor ligands, the complex can switch between low-spin and high-spin states in response to temperature, pressure or light: **spin crossover**. The high-spin state, with its populated e_g* orbitals, has longer metal–ligand bonds (about 0.2 Å) and higher entropy, so it is favored at high temperature, and the switch is accompanied by a change in color and magnetism. It is explored for molecular switches and data storage; hemoglobin undergoes a related change when Fe(II) binds O₂.

example.title: Moments and spin states
example.problem: [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ is diamagnetic, but [CoF₆]³⁻ has a moment of 5.3 μ_B. Explain.
example.solution: Both contain Co³⁺, d⁶. With strong-field NH₃, Δₒ > P and the complex is low-spin t₂g⁶ with no unpaired electrons (diamagnetic). With weak-field F⁻, Δₒ < P, so high-spin t₂g⁴e_g² with four unpaired electrons (μ_so = 4.90 μ_B, and the observed 5.3 includes an orbital contribution).

check.a: Δₒ is comparable with the pairing energy, and temperature, pressure or light tips the balance

sections.title: Electronic spectra and color
body: A complex looks colored when it absorbs part of visible light (400–700 nm) and transmits the rest. The observed color is the complement of the color absorbed.
The absorptions are of two kinds.

list: **d–d (ligand field) transitions** move an electron from t₂g to e_g, with energy near Δₒ. [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ (d¹) shows one band at 493 nm, corresponding to Δₒ = 20,300 cm⁻¹ = 243 kJ mol⁻¹, and is violet. In centrosymmetric complexes these transitions are **Laporte-forbidden** (g → g), so they are weak (ε about 1–100 M⁻¹ cm⁻¹), and they are even weaker when **spin-forbidden**: high-spin Mn(II) (d⁵, every transition changes the spin) is a very pale pink. Tetrahedral complexes, with no inversion center, are more intense (ε about 100–1000: [CoCl₄]²⁻ is deep blue). A d⁰ or d¹⁰ ion has no d–d transitions, so Zn²⁺ and Sc³⁺ are colorless.

**Charge-transfer transitions** move an electron between metal and ligand orbitals, and are allowed and very intense (ε of 10³–10⁵). In **LMCT** (ligand-to-metal) an electron goes from the ligand to the metal, as in the deep purple of permanganate MnO₄⁻ (d⁰) and chromate CrO₄²⁻ (yellow) and the red of [Fe(SCN)(H₂O)₅]²⁺. In **MLCT** (metal-to-ligand) an electron goes from a metal d orbital into a ligand π* orbital: [Ru(bipy)₃]²⁺ is orange (λ_max 452 nm, ε about 14,000) and its long-lived excited state is used in solar cells and photocatalysis.

body.h: Interpreting spectra of more than one d electron

body: With two or more d electrons, electron repulsion produces several excited states with the same electron configuration, and multiple bands. **Tanabe–Sugano diagrams** plot the energies of all the states (in units of the Racah repulsion parameter B) against Δₒ/B for each d^n configuration, so the positions of the bands give both Δₒ and B. A simpler **Orgel diagram** covers weak-field cases. For octahedral [V(H₂O)₆]³⁺ (d²) the three allowed spin bands are at 17,200, 25,600 and about 38,000 cm⁻¹. The **nephelauxetic effect** (“cloud-expanding”) is the reduction of B in the complex below its value in the free ion (B/B₀ < 1): electrons delocalize onto the ligands, which reduces repulsion. B/B₀ falls in the order F⁻ > H₂O > NH₃ > en > Cl⁻ > CN⁻ > Br⁻ > I⁻, and the bigger the reduction, the more covalent the bond.

example.title: From a spectrum to Δₒ
example.problem: [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ absorbs maximally at 493 nm. Find Δₒ in cm⁻¹ and kJ mol⁻¹, and the color.

eq: Δₒ = 20,300 cm⁻¹ × 11.96 J mol⁻¹ per cm⁻¹ = 243 kJ mol⁻¹

solution: The complex absorbs blue-green light (493 nm) and transmits red and violet, so it looks violet-purple.

summary: In an octahedral field, d orbitals split into t₂g (−0.4Δₒ) and e_g (+0.6Δₒ). LFSE = (−0.4 n_t₂g + 0.6 n_e_g)Δₒ plus pairing energy. Strong fields (Δₒ > P) give low-spin d⁴–d⁷ complexes.
Spectrochemical series: halides < H₂O < NH₃ < en < CN⁻ < CO. Δ increases with metal oxidation state and down a group.
Δₜ = (4/9)Δₒ and tetrahedral complexes are high-spin. d⁸ with strong ligands (and 4d/5d metals) are square planar. d⁹, d⁴ (high-spin) and d⁷ (low-spin) show Jahn–Teller distortion.
π-donors lower Δ, and π-acceptors (back-bonding) raise it.
μ_so = √(n(n + 2)) μ_B gives the unpaired electron count. Cooperative magnetism and spin crossover occur in solids.
d–d bands are weak (Laporte, and spin-forbidden); charge-transfer bands (LMCT, MLCT) are intense. Absorbed λ gives Δ, and the observed color is the complement.

problems.q: Give the d-electron configuration, spin state, unpaired electrons and LFSE (in Δₒ) for (a) [Cr(H₂O)₆]³⁺, (b) [Mn(H₂O)₆]²⁺, (c) [Ni(H₂O)₆]²⁺, (d) [Co(CN)₆]³⁻.
problems.solution: (a) d³: t₂g³, 3 unpaired, LFSE −1.2. (b) d⁵ with weak H₂O: t₂g³e_g², 5 unpaired, LFSE 0. (c) d⁸: t₂g⁶e_g², 2 unpaired, LFSE −1.2. (d) d⁶ with strong CN⁻: t₂g⁶, 0 unpaired, LFSE −2.4 + 2P.

problems.q: Why is [NiCl₄]²⁻ tetrahedral and paramagnetic while [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻ is square planar and diamagnetic?
problems.solution: Both are Ni(II), d⁸. The weak-field chloride gives a small splitting, so the complex takes the less crowded tetrahedral geometry with two unpaired electrons. Strong-field cyanide gives a large splitting of the d_{x²−y²} orbital in a square planar field, so the eight electrons pair in the lower four orbitals and leave d_{x²−y²} empty: diamagnetic.
problems.a: Weak-field Cl⁻ gives tetrahedral and paramagnetic. Strong-field CN⁻ gives square planar and diamagnetic.

problems.q: [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ has its first d–d band at 475 nm. Calculate Δₒ in cm⁻¹ and kJ mol⁻¹. For the low-spin d⁶ configuration give the LFSE (omit P).
problems.solution: Δₒ = 1/(475 × 10⁻⁷ cm) = 21,050 cm⁻¹ = 21,050 × 11.96 = 252 kJ mol⁻¹. LFSE = −2.4Δₒ = −605 kJ mol⁻¹, before correcting for pairing.
problems.a: Δₒ ≈ 21,000 cm⁻¹ = 252 kJ mol⁻¹; LFSE ≈ −2.4Δₒ ≈ −605 kJ mol⁻¹ (before the pairing correction).

problems.q: A Cu(II) complex has μ = 1.9 μ_B and is blue. Give the number of unpaired electrons, and say why its geometry is probably distorted.
problems.solution: The spin-only value for one unpaired electron is 1.73 μ_B, and orbital contribution raises it to about 1.9: d⁹, one unpaired electron. d⁹ in an octahedral field has an e_g³ configuration (degenerate), which gives a strong Jahn–Teller elongation.
problems.a: One unpaired electron; Jahn–Teller distortion (tetragonal elongation).
